title: Disney Animation: The Illusion of Life (rev. ed. The Illusion of Life: Disney Animation, 1995)
doi_isbn: ISBN 0-7868-6070-7 (1995 Disney Editions); 1981 Abbeville ISBN reported inconsistently across catalogues
key_findings: Origin of the 12 principles of animation (squash & stretch, anticipation, staging, straight ahead/pose to pose, follow through & overlapping action, slow in/out, arcs, secondary action, timing, exaggeration, solid drawing, appeal) — as summarised by Lasseter 1987 and Chang & Ungar 1993 who both cite it
Head-turn timing table (0–10 inbetweens between two extremes change the meaning of the same two drawings) is quoted from this book in Lasseter 1987
practical_applications: Vocabulary for every animation note in rig.js / GUIDE §4
Timing table drives ANIMATION_MOTION_LIBRARY anim.head_turn
limitations: Book not read this session; content known only through Lasseter 1987 and Chang & Ungar 1993 quotations
Craft knowledge from Disney feature practice, not experimental science

title: The Animator's Survival Kit (expanded edition)
key_findings: Library TOC lists a chapter 'Timing, staggers, wave and whip'
Standard reference for the contact/down/passing/up walk method (as already summarised in curriculum 06 from course material that cites it)
practical_applications: Walk, stagger, wave/whip entries in ANIMATION_MOTION_LIBRARY follow its vocabulary
limitations: Not read this session; frame numbers attributed to it in the wild must be checked against the book

title: Timing for Animation (2nd ed., updated by Tom Sito)
authors: Harold Whitaker; John Halas; Tom Sito
key_findings: Cited by Lasseter 1987 (ref 30) for: timing defines weight; heavy objects need more time to start/stop; light objects accelerate quickly; the effect of weight depends on spacing, not on the drawing
Faster actions must still be readable: too little time and the move is over before the audience notices
practical_applications: Weight → frame count rules in module 16 and library durations
limitations: Content known via Lasseter's quotation of the 1981 edition; 2009 edition not read

title: Principles of Traditional Animation Applied to 3D Computer Animation
key_findings: Timing gives meaning: two head drawings with 0 inbetweens = hit by a tremendous force; 1 = hit by a brick; 2 = nervous tic; 3 = dodging; 4 = crisp order; 5 = friendly 'over here'; 6 = sees something desirable; 7 = tries to get a better look; 8 = searches the shelf; 9 = appraises thoughtfully; 10 = stretches a sore muscle (quoting Thomas & Johnston)
Spend enough time (but no more) on anticipation, action and reaction; too much → attention wanders, too little → idea missed
Wally B.'s zip-off action is only 3–4 frames, readable because the anticipation is long enough; the more the audience expects, the faster the action can be
Staging: one idea at a time; in a still scene the eye goes to movement, in a busy scene to something still; Luxo Jr. animated with silhouette in mind

Follow-through rate differs by material/mass (light antennae drag slightly, heavy flexible feet drag far, even staying on screen frames after the body left); overlap: feet left 1–2 frames apart; never bring one action to a full stop before the next starts
Pose-to-pose with keyframes for acting; straight-ahead for wild action
practical_applications: anim.head_turn timing table; anim.anticipation_strike readability rule; follow-through lags per material in rig.js puppets
limitations: Practitioner paper in a peer-reviewed venue; no user testing
PDF text extracted from a scan; sections 2.1–2.11 read, figures not seen

title: Animation: From Cartoons to the User Interface
key_findings: Groups Disney principles into solidity, exaggeration, reinforcement for UI motion
Cartoon motion blur lets objects move fast and stay comprehensible; dissolve-through-others keeps the sense of solidity
Slow in/slow out, arcs and follow through reinforce the illusion and reduce surprise; anticipation = small contrary motion before the main move
practical_applications: Basis for applying animation principles to kinetic type and UI-style motion in FD18
limitations: Design report on the Self UI, no controlled experiment
Extracted full text; sections 2.1–2.3 read

title: Perceptual Evaluation of Cartoon Physics: Accuracy, Attention, Appeal
authors: Marcos Garcia; John Dingliana; Carol O'Sullivan
key_findings: Squash-and-stretch stylisation significantly improved users' accuracy in predicting bouncing-object trajectories, especially for high elasticity and low information
No evidence that cartoon physics directed attention in a multi-object word task
A game with cartoon physics was chosen as more appealing almost twice as often as the unstylised one
practical_applications: Squash & stretch helps the viewer read physics (where a thing will land) — use on product drops, bouncing logos
limitations: Small samples (one experiment N=24); simple objects, not characters
Abstract + method lines read only

title: Perceptual plausibility of exaggerated realistic motion
authors: Filipp Schmidt; Laura Noejovich; George Chakalos; Flip Phillips
key_findings: Bouncing balls with small amounts of squash & stretch were judged as plausible as physically veridical motion
When ball type was unspecified observers tolerated large exaggeration; when material was indicated the acceptable range narrowed but still exceeded physical possibility
Authors argue exaggeration can bridge the uncanny valley for artificial depictions of physics
practical_applications: Realistic product renders (glasses, bottles) can take mild squash on landing without looking fake; reduce exaggeration when the material is obvious (glass, metal)
limitations: Simple bouncing balls only; abstract read

title: Yo!: Enriching Emotional Quality of Single-Button Messengers through Kinetic Typography
doi_isbn: DIS 2016, ACM 978-1-4503-4031-1 (doi 10.1145/2901790.2901835 per PDF header, partly legible)
key_findings: 20 participants rated 31 animated texts (8 animation types × 3 speeds × 3 dynamics, orthogonal design) on 6 emotions + Affect Grid
Animation TYPE was the most important factor for conveyed emotion; speed and dynamics acted mainly as 'amplifiers'

Vertical/jumping → excitement quadrant (happiness, surprise); horizontal/expansion → stress (anger, fear, surprise); vibration/flopping/shimmy → low-mood quadrant (sadness, fear, disappointment); pendulum ≈ neutral
practical_applications: Pick the motion TYPE of kinetic text by emotion first, then tune speed; see FD18 kinetic typography table
limitations: N=20, Korean young adults, one word ('Yo'), phone display
Results section read from extracted PDF text; author list incomplete

title: Creating Emordle: Animating Word Cloud for Emotion Expression
authors: Liwenhan Xie; Xinhuan Shu; Jeon Cheol Su; Yun Wang; Siming Chen; Huamin Qu
key_findings: People generally agreed on emotions conveyed by well-crafted text animations (crowdsourced study 1)
Two global factors — randomness of the animation (entropy) and speed — fine-tuned emotional intensity (study 2)
practical_applications: Calm/sad text = low entropy, slow; anger/fear = high entropy, fast
limitations: Abstract only; N not reported in abstract; word clouds not single titles

title: The kinetic typography engine: an extensible system for animating expressive text
authors: Johnny C. Lee; Jodi Forlizzi; Scott E. Hudson
key_findings: UIST 2002 system paper: a Java library for composing expressive text animation from reusable behaviours; defines kinetic typography as expression with animated text
practical_applications: Composable behaviour idea = our GSAP text presets
limitations: Bibliographic + project page only; no perceptual results read

title: Motion (Material Components for Android — M3 easing, duration and spring tokens)
key_findings: Standard cubic-bezier(0.2,0,0,1); standard decelerate (0,0,0,1); standard accelerate (0.3,0,1,1); emphasized decelerate (0.05,0.7,0.1,1); emphasized accelerate (0.3,0,0.8,0.15); emphasized = 2-segment path; linear (0,0,1,1)
Duration tokens 50–1000 ms (short1 50 … medium2 300 … long2 500 … extraLong4 1000); duration should grow with area/distance travelled
Spring tokens: fast spatial damping 0.9 stiffness 1400; default spatial 0.9/700; slow spatial 0.9/300; effects (colour/opacity) damping 1 = no overshoot
practical_applications: Exact ease values for kinetic type and UI-style product motion (FD18 table)
limitations: Design-system convention for apps, not perceptual evidence; values may change between versions

title: Human Interface Guidelines — Motion
key_findings: Add motion purposefully; don't add motion for its own sake; gratuitous motion can distract or cause physical discomfort
Aim for brevity and precision in feedback animations; avoid motion on frequent interactions
Make motion optional; motion should not be the only carrier of important information
Realistic feedback motion follows gestures/expectations; let people cancel motion; games: consistent 30–60 fps
practical_applications: Motion budget rule in FD18: one purposeful move per element; captions must not rely on motion alone
limitations: App UI guidance; video has no 'cancel' but the purpose/brevity rules transfer

title: Designing Fluid Interfaces (WWDC 2018 session 803)
key_findings: Springs described by damping ratio (1 = critically damped, no bounce; lower = bounce) and response (period of the undamped system) instead of mass/stiffness
practical_applications: Spring vocabulary for overshoot settles (anim.settle)
limitations: Only search summaries read; numeric values seen on third-party sites not verified

title: GSAP 3 Docs — Eases
key_findings: Core eases: none, power1–4, back, bounce, circ, elastic, expo, sine, steps; each (except none/steps) with .in/.out/.inOut
power1=quad, power2=cubic, power3=quart, power4=quint/strong
Default ease is power1.out; rough/slow/expoScale in EasePack; CustomEase/CustomBounce/CustomWiggle are extra plugins
practical_applications: Ease names used in rig.js and in every library entry's gsap hint
limitations: Parameter syntax (back.out(1.7), elastic amplitude/period) not documented on this page

title: GSAP 3 Docs — CustomEase
key_findings: CustomEase.create also recognises standard cubic-bezier strings, e.g. CustomEase.create("easeName", ".17,.67,.83,.67")
Accepts SVG path data (M, C, S, L, Z); not in core — must be loaded separately
practical_applications: Use Material/CSS cubic-bezier values inside GSAP timelines (HyperFrames)
limitations: Licensing/pricing not stated on the page

title: CSS Easing Functions Level 1 (Candidate Recommendation Draft, 13 Feb 2023)
key_findings: steps(n, jump-start|jump-end|jump-none|jump-both) defines stepped timing (= animating 'on twos' as an easing)
practical_applications: Exact reference values; steps() for on-2s/on-3s looks in CSS
limitations: Draft standard; defines math, not aesthetics

title: Creating Usability with Motion: The UX in Motion Manifesto
key_findings: 12 UX motion principles: easing, offset & delay, parenting, transformation, value change, masking, overlay, cloning, obscuration, parallax, dimensionality, dolly & zoom
Offset & delay (derived from Disney follow-through/overlap) separates elements so they are not read as one group
practical_applications: Stagger rules for kinetic type and product-feature lists
limitations: Practitioner essay; read through secondary summaries only

title: Audio-Vision: Sound on Screen (2nd ed., trans. Claudia Gorbman, foreword Walter Murch)
doi_isbn: Columbia University Press 2019 (1st Eng. ed. 1994; French 1990)
key_findings: Added value: the expressive/informative value sound adds to an image, which seems to come from the image itself
Synchresis: involuntary fusion of a sound and a visual event when they coincide, independent of rational logic (dubbed punch example)
practical_applications: Any sound placed exactly on a visual accent will be heard as that object's sound — the basis of Foley and cartoon SFX
See also creative-intelligence/knowledge/sound key Chion1994_AudioVision
limitations: Book not read; definitions from reviews and secondary academic articles

title: Rec. ITU-R BT.1359-1 Relative timing of sound and vision for broadcasting
key_findings: Detectability threshold about +45 ms (sound early) to −125 ms (sound late); acceptability about +90 to −185 ms
Viewers are more sensitive to sound leading picture than lagging
Cites ITU-R BR.265: film sound-picture location within ± half a frame (~22 ms at 24 fps)
practical_applications: SFX may sit 0–2 frames after the visual hit safely; sound more than ~1 frame early is detectable
limitations: Broadcast lip-sync tests; read via search summary of the ITU PDF

title: Temporal window of integration in auditory-visual speech perception
authors: Virginie van Wassenhove; Ken W. Grant; David Poeppel
key_findings: ~200 ms audiovisual integration window for speech, asymmetric (tolerates visual-lead / audio-lag more than audio-lead)
practical_applications: Lip-sync tolerance: mouth may lead the audio by a frame or two (rig talk leads by 1 frame)
limitations: Speech syllables in lab; abstract-level reading

title: Audiovisual temporal integration for complex speech, object-action, animal call, and musical stimuli (in Multisensory Object Perception in the Primate Brain, Springer, pp. 95–121)
key_findings: Temporal window of audiovisual integration is several hundred ms wide and asymmetric (larger when vision leads)
Window depends on stimulus type/complexity; judgments more precise for speech than for music clips
practical_applications: Music-performance footage tolerates slightly looser sync than dialogue; dialogue is the strictest
limitations: Chapter abstract only

title: Perceptual judgment of the relationship between musical and visual components in film
authors: Scott D. Lipscomb; Roger A. Kendall
key_findings: Using five scenes from a commercial film with alternative scores, a musical soundtrack can change the 'meaning' of a film presentation
practical_applications: Same footage + different music = different story; test 2 music options on key scenes
limitations: Repository abstract; year listed 1994 in citations, 1996 in the repository

title: Cognition of musical and visual accent structure alignment in film and animation (PhD dissertation, UCLA)
key_findings: Asked what determines accent in sound and image, and whether precise alignment is necessary for an effective combination
Defined consonant (same rate, aligned), out-of-phase and dissonant alignment conditions; tested with VAME and similarity judgments
practical_applications: Vocabulary for beat-sync choices: consonant (on-beat), out-of-phase (same tempo, offset), dissonant (unrelated)
limitations: Dissertation abstract only; results not read

title: Congruence-Association Model and Experiments in Film Music: Toward Interdisciplinary Collaboration
key_findings: Audience tries to build a meaningful story from all channels; congruence = shared structural features (e.g., accents) directs attention; association = music's emotional meaning colours a neutral scene
Model grew from Marshall & Cohen 1988 (music + geometric shapes)
practical_applications: Structural congruence (accents aligned) pulls attention to the moving thing; associative meaning sets mood
limitations: Read through citing papers only; critics (Ireland) say 'congruence' is used loosely

title: Musical soundtracks as a schematic influence on the cognitive processing of filmed events
key_findings: Three ambiguous film clips shown with positive, negative or no music: interpretation of the clips followed the music's valence; the author explains it as music acting as an interpretive schema for the visual events
practical_applications: Music must be chosen for the meaning of the scene, not only its energy
limitations: Abstract/citation summaries only

title: Edit Blindness: The relationship between attention and global change blindness in dynamic scenes
authors: Tim J. Smith; John M. Henderson
key_findings: Edits following continuity rules were missed more than edits breaking them
About a quarter of cuts between two viewpoints of the same scene went undetected, rising to a third when the cut coincided with a sudden onset of motion
practical_applications: Cut on motion onset (and on a sound) to hide the cut
limitations: Abstract and citing summaries; Hollywood-style clips

title: Match-action: the role of motion and audio in creating global change blindness in film
authors: Tim J. Smith; Janice Martin-Portugues Santacreu
key_findings: Existing match-action cuts in feature films were missed more often (32.4%) in a cut-detection task than other cuts
Edit blindness mostly disappeared when the audio was removed — continuous sound across a cut hides it
practical_applications: Keep the sound bed continuous across cuts (L/J cuts, ambience) to make cuts invisible
limitations: Search-summary level only

title: On-Beat/Off-Beat: Visual Responses to Audio-Visual Asynchrony in Music Videos
key_findings: Reports empirical cognitive and attentional differences between viewers of music videos cut on-beat vs off-beat (direction of the effect not read)
practical_applications: Evidence that beat alignment of cuts changes viewing, but which way must be checked before claiming 'on-beat is better'
limitations: Search snippet of the abstract only; findings direction unknown

title: The impact of music and stretched time on pupillary responses and eye movements in slow-motion film scenes
key_findings: No systematic effect of music on eye movements in slow-motion scenes, but music increased arousal (pupil size)
Review section: gaze consistency is highest for strongly edited films; cuts drive gaze more than context
practical_applications: Music changes feeling more than where people look — guide the eye with picture, the mood with music
limitations: Search summary only

title: In the Blink of an Eye (2nd ed.)
doi_isbn: Silman-James Press (a secondary review prints ISBN 1-879595-62-2 — unverified)
key_findings: Rule of Six for a cut, ranked: emotion 51%, story 23%, rhythm 10%, eye-trace 7%, 2D plane 5%, 3D space 4% (weights as reported by secondary sources)
practical_applications: When a beat-cut fights the emotion, emotion wins (rhythm ranks third)
limitations: Book not read; weights from secondary summaries; craft not science

title: Sound Design: The Expressive Power of Music, Voice and Sound Effects in Cinema
key_findings: Practitioner textbook covering psychoacoustics, music theory, voice and film analyses with exercises
practical_applications: Background reading for SFX layering and voice design
limitations: Bibliographic only

title: On the Track: A Guide to Contemporary Film Scoring (2nd ed.)
key_findings: Standard film-scoring text with parts on spotting the film and on timings and clicks (click tracks) — per its index/TOC
practical_applications: Spotting-session vocabulary: hit points, click tempo, catching vs playing through
limitations: TOC/index only; no page-level content read

title: The Visual Story: Creating the Visual Structure of Film, TV, and Digital Media (3rd ed.)
key_findings: Organises visual structure around contrast & affinity of basic visual components (space, line, shape, tone, colour, movement, rhythm) across a story
practical_applications: Storyboard intensity graph: plan where movement/rhythm contrast peaks (FD25)
limitations: Bibliographic (TOC lists Contrast & Affinity, Rhythm)

title: Film Directing Shot by Shot: Visualizing from Concept to Screen
key_findings: Combines story analysis with compositional strategy, illustrated with storyboards used on actual films; alternative shot layouts side by side
practical_applications: Practice: board the same scene 2–3 ways and compare (FD25 exercise)
limitations: Bibliographic; overhead-diagram content not confirmed this session

title: The Art of the Storyboard: A Filmmaker's Introduction (2nd ed.)
key_findings: Introductory text on storyboarding for live action and animation (Focal Press)
practical_applications: Panel drawing conventions (arrows, frame lines) in STORYBOARD_TEMPLATE
limitations: Bibliographic only

title: Storyboard Pro — How to Create an Animatic / Timeline view / Export (docs, v6–7)
key_findings: Animatic = panels timed on a timeline with sound clips, animated camera moves and transitions
Changing one panel's duration ripples later panels by default; frame-level add/remove per panel
Export to movie, EDL/XML/AAF (keeps timing and sound for editors), or Harmony scenes (camera moves, drawings)
practical_applications: Our animatic = still frames + TTS + rig cam in HyperFrames (FD25 pipeline)
limitations: Search-result summaries of the docs; some doc URLs 404 at fetch time

title: How to Make a Shot List / Shot list templates / Shot Designer
key_findings: Typical shot-list columns: scene #, shot #, subject, description, camera, shot size, shot type, movement, equipment, lens, special equipment (+ frame rate, angle, sound, location in Shot Designer)
Floor plan shows camera, actors and key props positions; shots grouped by camera/lighting setup to schedule
practical_applications: SHOT_LIST_TEMPLATE columns
limitations: Commercial tool vendor; search summaries

title: Multiplane camera
key_findings: Layers painted on separate planes at different distances, moved at different speeds (nearest fastest) to create parallax
Reiniger/Koch (Prince Achmed, 1926), Iwerks 1933, Fleischer Setback 1934 (3D miniature sets), Disney/Garity 1937 up to 7 layers, tested on The Old Mill (Oscar) then Snow White
Opposite-direction movement of fore/background suggests rotation; replaced by digital multiplane (CAPS); Little Mermaid (1989) last physical use at Disney
practical_applications: rig.js layer --d depth parallax = digital multiplane
limitations: Tertiary source; verify history details before publishing

title: The Anime Machine: A Media Theory of Animation
key_findings: Anime as a 'multiplanar image': layers composited and slid relative to each other
'Animetism' (sliding flat layers, lateral movement) vs 'cinematism' (movement into depth along one-point perspective), after Virilio
practical_applications: Lateral layer slides (pans across layered BG) are a native anime look; push-ins into depth read more 'cinematic'
limitations: Reviews/catalogue only

title: Studio Ghibli Layout Designs: Understanding the Secrets of Takahata/Miyazaki Animation (exhibition, MOT Tokyo 2008, toured)
authors: Museum of Contemporary Art Tokyo / Studio Ghibli
key_findings: ~1,300 layout drawings shown; the layout is the blueprint of each shot setting framing, background and character movement
practical_applications: Layout stage in FD17/FD25: framing + BG + movement paths decided per cut before animation
limitations: Exhibition listings only

title: Exposure Sheets (animation school notes) + Wikipedia 'Exposure sheet'
key_findings: X-sheet (dope sheet) = frame-by-frame timing + camera instructions; camera column notes truck-in/out, pans, field size (FLD) and N/S, E/W position on the field guide
practical_applications: Camera notation in STORYBOARD_TEMPLATE (TI/TO, pan, field)
limitations: Search summaries

title: J cut and L cut (Adobe Creative Cloud guide)
key_findings: Split edits: J-cut = next shot's audio starts before its picture; L-cut = previous audio continues over the new picture; also called audio lead/advance
practical_applications: sync.j_cut / sync.l_cut in SOUND_SYNC_LIBRARY
limitations: Search summary

title: Presence (sound recording) / What is room tone
key_findings: Room tone = the location's 'silence' with no dialogue; record ≥30 s per location/setup; used by dialogue editors to fill gaps so edits do not sound choppy
practical_applications: Never cut to digital zero inside a scene; generate a room-tone bed for TTS dialogue
limitations: Practitioner/encyclopedic summaries
